nameStory: This microscopic green algae doesn't have a true common name since it's mainly known to scientists and microscope enthusiasts. The scientific name Micrasterias comes from Greek words meaning 'small star,' perfectly describing its intricate, star-like symmetrical shape. It was named after Thomas, likely a botanist who first studied this particular species.
description: Micrasterias thomasiana is a single-celled green algae that lives in freshwater ponds and lakes. Despite being microscopic (you'd need a microscope to see its details), it's actually one of the larger single-celled organisms, reaching about 100-200 micrometers across. It has a distinctive flat, disc-like shape that's perfectly symmetrical, looking like an ornate snowflake or intricate doily when viewed under magnification. This tiny organism is actually quite beautiful, with elaborate lobes and decorative patterns radiating from its center.

idTips.label: Symmetrical star shape
idTips.description: The cell forms a perfect bilateral symmetry with elaborate lobes extending outward like points of a decorative star

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Bright green color from chlorophyll, visible even at low magnifications as tiny emerald specks in water samples

idTips.label: Constricted center
idTips.description: The cell has a narrow waist or constriction in the middle where the two halves meet, like a figure-eight pinched at the center

idTips.label: Smooth cell wall
idTips.description: The outer edge appears smooth and glassy under magnification, without spines or rough textures

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Large enough to see as individual green specks with a hand lens, but requires a microscope to see the star-like details

habitat: Found in clean, still freshwater environments like pristine ponds, quiet lake edges, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers slightly acidic, nutrient-poor waters and is often found among aquatic plants or floating near the surface in shallow areas. This species indicates good water quality since it's sensitive to pollution.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water warms, appearing as faint green tinge in pond water. Best time to collect samples as organisms are actively reproducing.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance in warm water, easily collected by gently scooping surface water or squeezing aquatic plants into a jar.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations declining as temperatures drop. May form resting stages to survive winter.
seasonality.winter: Dormant or present in very low numbers under ice cover, difficult to find and identify.

funFact: Despite being a single cell, Micrasterias thomasiana is an accomplished architect that can rebuild its entire elaborate shape if damaged, taking about 24 hours to regenerate missing lobes with mathematical precision!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Micrasterias species, which all share the basic star shape but differ in their specific lobe patterns and ornamentations. Look for the specific arrangement and number of projections, and remember that each species has its own unique 'fingerprint' of decorative details.
contextualKnowledge: Though called an 'algae,' Micrasterias is actually more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds. These organisms are popular among microscopists and are often featured in competitions for photomicrography due to their incredible beauty and symmetry.
compareHints: Micrasterias thomasiana has smoother, less ornate lobes compared to the heavily decorated M. denticulata or the deeply divided M. pinnatifida. Unlike M. truncata which has squared-off ends, M. thomasiana has more rounded, graceful projections. It's generally smaller and simpler than the elaborate M. furcata with its forked extensions.
